## What it is

- A long-necked, **unfretted** lute with a gourd body and a platform bridge with a rounded surface; the strings are always plucked at full length (Garland, p. 332; Wikipedia, "Tanpura"). Usually **four** strings (Garland: four or five), held upright; it probably developed from the fretted tambur, and appears as a drone in 17th-century Mughal paintings (Garland, p. 332).
- It plays no melody: it holds the **drone** under a singer or player. Usual tuning **Pa-sa-sa-Sa** (5-8-8-1; Garland gives G-c-c-C, p. 355, for the Karnatak tambura); **Ma** for ragas without Pa; **Dha** or **Ni** for ragas without Pa and shuddha Ma (Wikipedia).
- These are living traditions with their own teachers, names and ways of playing. The site's sound is a sketch from a few physics ideas, not the instrument; anything not from a source named on this page is marked unverified.

## How it sounds

- **Jawari**: the string grazes a wide, curved bridge; as its swing dies, the touching point creeps up the bridge's slope, and that makes a long, moving buzz of overtones (Wikipedia, "Tanpura", "Sitar"). Here the upper partials **grow** while the lowest ones fade: the opposite of a guitar string. The amounts are the site's.
- A **thread** (juari, jiva; cotton in Wikipedia, silk in Garland, p. 355) between string and bridge moves the touching place and changes which overtones sing: a rich blend of overtones and a much longer ring (Garland, pp. 332, 355; Wikipedia). Turn **Thread** and listen.
- The four strings are plucked one after another, over and over, in order (Garland, p. 355); Karnatak players often pluck long-short-short-long, unrelated to the tempo or tala (Garland, p. 355). Here 1-2-3-4 and a rest at an even pace (the site's spacing, unverified).

## Works Cited

<!-- works-cited: written by scripts/works-cited.py -->
::: {.works-cited}
Miner, Allyn. "Musical Instruments: Northern Area." *The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music*, vol. 5, *South Asia: The Indian Subcontinent*, edited by Alison Arnold, Garland, 2000, pp. 331-49. Tambura: unfretted long-necked lute, gourd, platform bridge with rounded surface and threads under the strings, rich in overtones, four or five strings tuned to the tonic and the fourth or fifth, probably from the tambur, a drone in 17th-century Mughal paintings (p. 332). Sitar: twenty movable arched frets, six or seven main strings, thirteen sympathetic strings on a small bridge of their own, portamento up to a fifth on a fret, curved bridge, mizrab, Shankar and Vilayat Khan styles (pp. 334-35); first written of in 1739, not Amir Khusrau (p. 335); bin eclipsed by the sitar (p. 333).

Reck, David B. "Musical Instruments: Southern Area." *The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music*, vol. 5, *South Asia: The Indian Subcontinent*, edited by Alison Arnold, Garland, 2000, pp. 350-70. Karnatak tambura: four strings Pa-Sa-Sa-low Sa (G-c-c-C), plucked in that order, often long-short-short-long unrelated to tala; silk jiva thread under each string on a convex bridge (p. 355).

"Sitar." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sitar). 18-21 strings, 6-7 played over curved movable frets, the rest sympathetic (tarb); two bridges; the wide rounded bridge and jawari; main string a fourth above Sa; Kharaj Pancham tuning; meend up to about seven semitones; instrumental style typically 13 sympathetic strings; Norwegian Wood, Love You To, Within You Without You, Paint It Black.

"Tanpura." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanpura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanpura). Four strings, 5-8-8-1 (Pa-sa-sa-Sa), Ma for ragas without Pa, Dha or Ni for ragas without Pa and shuddha Ma (Marwa, Hindol); jivari: the curved bridge, grazing contact creeping up the slope over 3-10 s; the cotton thread shifts it; Miraj and Tanjore styles; electronic tanpuras.

Wade, Bonnie C. "Visual Sources." *The Garland Encyclopedia of World Music*, vol. 5, *South Asia: The Indian Subcontinent*, edited by Alison Arnold, Garland, 2000, pp. 298-311. The tambur lost its frets and became the drone tambura / tanpura (p. 310).

**For students**

"Love You To." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_You_To](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_You_To). Sitar, tabla and tambura; the first Beatles song fully in the Indian classical style.

"Tomorrow Never Knows." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomorrow_Never_Knows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomorrow_Never_Knows). A C drone on tambura.

"Within You Without You." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Within_You_Without_You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Within_You_Without_You). Sitar, tambura, dilruba, tabla; three tamburas giving a dense jivari (Hannan).
:::
